title: Work–energy theorem and complete force accounting

units.content:
## 9. Work-Energy Theorem

The work done on a particle by the net resultant force equals the change in its kinetic energy:

$$W_{\text{net}} = K_f - K_i = \Delta K \quad \text{--- (i)}$$

This theorem holds generally for both constant and variable forces, along arbitrary curved paths, in any inertial frame of reference.

### Partitioning Forces
Decomposing the total work into conservative ($W_c$), non-conservative ($W_{NC}$), and other external/pseudo forces ($W_{\text{oth}}$):

$$W_c + W_{NC} + W_{\text{oth}} = \Delta K \quad \text{--- (ii)}$$

Substituting $W_c = -\Delta U$:
$$-\Delta U + W_{NC} + W_{\text{oth}} = \Delta K$$
$$W_{NC} + W_{\text{oth}} = \Delta K + \Delta U = \Delta(K + U) \quad \text{--- (iii)}$$

Defining the total **Mechanical Energy** $E = K + U$:
$$\mathbf{W_{NC} + W_{\text{oth}} = \Delta E}$$

If only conservative forces perform work ($W_{NC} = 0, W_{\text{oth}} = 0$):
$$\Delta E = 0 \implies E = K + U = \text{constant (Conservation of Mechanical Energy)}$$

### 3D Calculus Derivation

![Work Along 3D Curved Path](images/fig_08_curved_path_work.svg)

Consider a particle moving along an arbitrary curved trajectory from point $P_1$ to $P_2$ under the action of net force $\vec{F}$:
$$W = \int_{P_1}^{P_2} \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = \int_{P_1}^{P_2} (F_x dx + F_y dy + F_z dz)$$

From Newton's second law along the $x$-direction:
$$F_x = m a_x = m \frac{dv_x}{dt}$$

Using the chain rule:
$$\frac{dv_x}{dt} = \frac{dv_x}{dx}\frac{dx}{dt} = v_x \frac{dv_x}{dx}$$

Substituting into the work integral:
$$\int_{P_1}^{P_2} F_x dx = \int_{P_1}^{P_2} m v_x \frac{dv_x}{dx} dx = \int_{v_{x1}}^{v_{x2}} m v_x dv_x = \frac{1}{2}m (v_{x2}^2 - v_{x1}^2)$$

Extending identically to $y$ and $z$ axes:
$$W = \frac{1}{2}m \left[ (v_{x2}^2 + v_{y2}^2 + v_{z2}^2) - (v_{x1}^2 + v_{y1}^2 + v_{z1}^2) \right] = \frac{1}{2}m (v_2^2 - v_1^2)$$

$$W = \frac{1}{2}mv_2^2 - \frac{1}{2}mv_1^2$$

Defining kinetic energy:
$$K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$

content.title: Work-Energy Theorem & Scalar Invariance
content.definition: The total work performed on a particle by the vector resultant of all forces acting upon it equals the net change in its kinetic energy: W_net = Delta K = 0.5 m v_f^2 - 0.5 m v_i^2.
canonical_rules: W_net includes all forces without exception: conservative, non-conservative, normal, and applied.
Kinetic energy is quadratic in velocity: K = 0.5 m v^2 = p^2 / (2m).
Stopping distance under constant braking friction scales quadratically with initial speed: s_stop = v_0^2 / (2 mu g).
operational_heuristics: Identify initial and final states; equate algebraic sum of work terms to K_f - K_i.
Eliminates the need for time-dependent kinematic integration when trajectory time is neither given nor sought.
boundary_conditions: v_f = 0: stopping condition W_net = -0.5 m v_0^2.

content.title: Net work sign tracks kinetic-energy change
content.badge_reason: Learners may attach energy change to one named force rather than to the combined work of all forces.
entry_assumptions: Can classify the sign of each force's work from its direction relative to displacement.
content.inferential_jump: The combined work of all acting forces determines the direction of kinetic-energy change: positive net work increases it, zero net work leaves it unchanged, and negative net work decreases it.

teaching_path.action: Keep the same initial motion and compare three cases whose combined work is positive, zero, or negative.
teaching_path.why_valid: Holding the initial state fixed isolates net-work sign as the changed condition.
teaching_path.output: case A: net work positive.  case B: net work zero.  case C: net work negative.

teaching_path.action: Match each net-work sign to whether the motion ends with greater, unchanged, or smaller kinetic energy.
teaching_path.why_valid: Net work is the energy transfer associated with the change in kinetic energy; the sign fixes the direction of that change.
teaching_path.output: positive -> kinetic energy increases.  zero -> unchanged.  negative -> decreases.

teaching_path.action: Use a braking situation as a check: the braking contribution points opposite the motion and the object slows.
teaching_path.why_valid: A familiar negative-work case should agree with a decrease in kinetic energy if the sign mapping is correct.
teaching_path.output: braking case: net work negative -> final kinetic energy lower than initial.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Only a positive force magnitude can increase kinetic energy; negative work cannot be represented physically.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A braking force acts opposite the motion. What sign is its work, and what should happen to kinetic energy?
misconceptions.repair: Combine the work of all acting forces to obtain net work, then match its sign to whether kinetic energy increases, stays unchanged, or decreases.

exit_task.prompt: For three otherwise comparable motions, the net work is described as positive, zero, and negative. State the corresponding direction of kinetic-energy change without calculating any energy value.

answer.summary: Positive net work means kinetic energy increases; zero means no change; negative means kinetic energy decreases.
reasoning: The comparison holds the starting motion fixed.
The sign of the combined work indicates the sign of the kinetic-energy change.
No individual force alone decides the result unless it is the only contributor.
answer.check: Use braking as the negative case: slowing must correspond to a decrease in kinetic energy.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer states only increase/no-change/decrease and contains no computed energy value.

content.research_contribution: Author-created sign mapping with no numerical work-energy equation.

predict.prompt: A moving object is braking. Before calculating anything, should the combined work over the braking interval correspond to increasing or decreasing kinetic energy?
predict.defensible_answer: Decreasing kinetic energy, so the net work over the interval is negative.

attempt.produces: A three-row mapping from net-work sign to kinetic-energy change, with the braking case used as one check.

rubric.criterion: Positive, zero, and negative net work map to increase, no change, and decrease respectively.
rubric.evidence_of: Separating sign from magnitude while preserving the energy-change direction.

rubric.criterion: The braking example is placed in the negative/decrease row.
rubric.evidence_of: Connecting the abstract sign mapping to a physical check.

accepted: 'Positive -> increase; zero -> unchanged; negative -> decrease. Braking belongs in negative -> decrease.'
rejected: 'Negative work means negative kinetic energy.' This confuses a change with the nonnegative energy quantity itself.

route.ask: During braking, is the force contribution along the motion or opposite it?
route.why_this_ask: The prior rung supplies the sign without introducing a new equation.

route.ask: Does the object end the interval moving with more or less kinetic energy than it began?
route.why_this_ask: The observable motion gives the direction of energy change.

route.ask: Which net-work sign belongs with that decrease?
route.why_this_ask: The learner links sign to change rather than memorizing the three-row table.

route.ask: What should zero net work imply in the same comparison?
route.why_this_ask: The zero case closes the mapping and tests that zero means no change rather than no energy.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path presents the sign mapping then checks braking. The learner route starts from braking, infers the negative/decrease connection, then generalizes to the complete mapping.

boundary_test.prompt: An object has nonzero kinetic energy throughout an interval but the net work over that interval is zero. Must the kinetic energy itself be zero?
boundary_test.answer: No. Zero net work means the kinetic energy does not change; it may remain nonzero.
boundary_test.confirms: The rule concerns change in kinetic energy, not the existence of kinetic energy.

content.meaning: Net work on a body equals its change in translational kinetic energy.

symbols.meaning: Final kinetic energy minus initial kinetic energy

conditions: The same body and reference frame are used for the force work and kinetic energies.

derivation.action: Compare the signed net work over an interval with the body's initial and final translational kinetic energies.
derivation.why_valid: The gate relation identifies net work as the change in K.

limits: This does not by itself choose which forces are included in the net work.

content.meaning: Translational kinetic energy of a body in the declared reference frame.
conditions: One declared reference frame is used.

derivation.action: Square the speed, multiply by mass, then take one half.
derivation.why_valid: REL-KINETIC-ENERGY owns the translational kinetic-energy relation.

limits: This record covers translational kinetic energy only.
checks: Doubling speed quadruples K at fixed mass.

oracle.description: How this exit answer is stood behind. Exactly one of: `verification`, naming a subject validator and binding its inputs to declared data; `held_by`, naming the known issue that explains why no oracle exists yet; or `no_numeric_claim`, saying why the answer asserts no computed value. Silence is not an option, because the exit answer is what a learner measures themselves against.

predict.description: Pose the decision before revealing anything.

prompt.description: The decision, posed so a learner can commit to an answer.

defensible_answer.description: The answer that commitment is judged against. A prompt with no defensible answer is a musing, not a prediction.

attempt.description: What the learner produces, and how it closes without a tutor.

produces.description: What the learner should construct, draw, discriminate or explain.

closure.description: Which form of closure this attempt uses. Each value demands something the others do not, so that none is a synonym an author can pick to avoid work: MODEL_RESPONSE requires model_response, CRITERIA requires rubric, and RUBRIC requires rubric with accepted and rejected examples -- the spec's 'a rubric plus representative accepted and rejected answers', which is the stronger claim of the three.

model_response.description: Closure as one response, where one is right.

rubric.description: Closure as a rubric, where several responses are valid.

rejected.description: Representative responses it rejects. A rubric with no rejected example has not been tested against anything.

task.description: Schema 0.2.0: the concrete reconstruction task the learner performs (a body, givens, numbers or a situation). `produces` says what the attempt should contain; `task` is what the learner is asked to do. Rendered as the Core1B attempt.

representation_ref.description: The representation of this task's own situation (its bodies and values), shown with the Core1B attempt. When absent, Core1B falls back to the first construction unit's (Core1A) figure, which depicts a different situation.

stage_refs.description: Stages of representation_ref safe to show before the attempt; default is the first stage only.

reconstruct.description: The correct construction reached the way a learner would reach it. Held as questions rather than statements: teaching_path is the expert's summary, and a reconstruct route made of statements is that summary under a different key, which is exactly how this product became the declarative one.

route.description: The sequence of asks. Order is meaning: each one is answerable only once the previous has been answered.

ask.description: A question that moves the learner one decision forward. A sentence with a question mark on it is not an ask; the learner must be able to get it wrong.

why_this_ask.description: Why this question rather than another at this point. An author who cannot say this has ordered the route by the expert's convenience.

from_step_ref.description: The teaching_path step this ask arrives at, where one exists. Absent means the learner's route genuinely departs from the expert's, which is why both are held.

differs_from_teaching_path.description: How the learner's route differs from the expert's construction. This is the sentence a reviewer checks the A/B claim against, so it may not restate the teaching path it claims to differ from.

prompt.description: A limiting case, reversal or edge condition.

confirms.description: What passing it establishes, stated so that a recall question cannot be passed off as a boundary test.

answer.description: What passing it looks like. The shared closure invariant has no exception for the last prompt in a cycle.

compact_anchor.description: Schema 0.2.0: the Core1 compact anchor, a one-line instance of the governing relation that makes the map usable before Core1A.

representation_ref.description: The representation of this compact anchor's own situation, shown on the Core1 map. When absent, Core1 falls back to the microtopic's first representation_refs entry, which is often shared across microtopics.

role.description: What the step does to the state. A DECLARE step fixes a convention or a domain and legitimately produces no computation; a TRANSFORM step changes the mathematical state and must show the changed state, not describe it; a VERIFY step checks a result against something already established.

source_ref.description: The source this step's claim rests on. Absent means the step is the author's own construction, which is legitimate and is not the same as source-supported.

content.description: One distinct decision/event of a microtopic's construction, taught as its own unit (Core1A) and reconstructed in Core1B.

crux_step_ref.description: The teaching_path step of this unit (one of its step_refs) that builds the move named questions in crux_question_refs turn on. The page marks that step, so a reader can see where the unit does the work the hard question needs.

misconception_indexes.description: Indexes into microtopic.misconceptions (wrong path, diagnose, repair).

migrated_from.description: Set by package_migrate.py when the unit was derived mechanically (e.g. 'teaching_path'); cleared when an author reviews it.

decision_from.description: Set instead of `decision` when the unit's decision is the microtopic's own field (migration); one source of truth, no copied text.

scene_instances.description: Concrete figures satisfying this representation. Everything above states what a figure of this kind must show; an instance states one actual figure, bound to the data it draws, so the library can compile a figure instead of only requiring one.

element.description: The part of the picture, named as required_elements names it.

symbol.description: The symbol it stands for, as the governing relation writes it.

in_words.description: The same thing said in words, which is the third leg of the bridge.

correspondence.description: The representation bridge. required_elements says what the picture must contain and the relation's symbols say what the algebra means, but nothing bound one to the other, so the correspondence a learner must make was asserted rather than held. Naming all three legs is what makes it explicit in both directions rather than a caption pointing one way.
